{{Short description|Japanese-American physicist}}
'''Gen Shirane''' ([[kanji]]: 白根 元 Shirane Gen; [[furigana]]: しらね げん; May 15, 1924 in [[Nishinomiya]],<ref name=AIP>{{cite web|title=G. Shirane|website=American Institute of Physics|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11609020.html}}</ref> [[Japan]] – 16 January 16, 2005 in [[Bellport, New York]]) was a Japanese-American experimental solid-state physicist, known for his investigations using neutron scattering as a probe of solids.<ref name=PhysicsToday>{{cite journal|author=Axel, John D.|author2=Birgeneau, Robert J.|author3=Blume, Martin|author4=Shapiro, Stephen M.|title=Obituary. Gen Shirane|journal=Physics Today|volume=58|issue=11|page=72|date=November 2005|doi=10.1063/1.2155771|doi-access=}}</ref> He lived most of his life in the USA.<ref>遠藤康夫『白根元博士を偲んで』　日本物理学会誌、Vol.60(8)、P.655、2005年 (Yasuo Endo “In Memory of Dr. Shirane” [[Physical Society of Japan]], Vol.60 (8), P.655, 2005)</ref>

==Biography==
At the [[University of Tokyo]], Shirane received his BE in engineering physics in 1944 and his DSc in physics in 1947 with a thesis on [[ferroelectrics]].<ref name=NAS/> He was from 1948 to 1952 a research associate in physics at the [[Tokyo Institute of Technology]]. At [[Pennsylvania State University]] he was from 1952 to 1955 a research associate and from 1955 to 1956 an assistant professor of physics. From 1956 to 1957 he was an associate physicist at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]. At Westinghouse Research Laboratories in Pittsburgh, he was from 1957 to 1958 a research physicist and from 1959 to 1963 an advising physicist. At Brookhaven National Laboratory he was from 1963 to 1968 a physicist and from 1968 to 2005 a senior physicist.<ref name=AIP/>

{{blockquote|Gen moved permanently to Brookhaven in 1963, as the Brookhaven High Flux Beam Reactor construction was being completed, and he contributed to the development of a suite of experimental instruments. The increased neutron flux made possible inelastic neutron-scattering experiments using the [[triple-axis spectrometer]] developed by [[Bertram Brockhouse]] in Canada. Optimizing the [[signal-to-noise ratio]] in these instruments is an art form in which Gen quickly established himself as a virtuoso, and that expertise led ultimately to his publication, with co-authors Stephen Shapiro and John Tranquada, of the definitive monograph on that subject.<ref name=PhysicsToday/>}}

{{blockquote|He worked on [[Spin wave|spin-wave]] dispersions and critical phenomena in ferromagnets, the soft phonon mode and the structural transition in [[Strontium titanate|SrTiO<sub>3</sub>]], spin fluctuations in low-dimensional antiferromagnets, electron-phonon coupling in superconducting [[Niobium–tin|Nb<sub>3</sub>Sn]], spin waves in [[chromium]], and eventually [[high-temperature superconductor]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Gen Shirane (1924–2005). Obituary written for Neutron News|website=Brookhaven National Laboratory|url=https://www.bnl.gov/cmpmsd/neutrons/Shirane_obituary_NN.asp}}</ref>}}

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Shirane with co-workers confirmed the soft mode theory of [[Philip Warren Anderson|P. W. Anderson]] and [[William Cochran (physicist)|W. Cochran]] and discovered new features of structural phase transitions beyond the soft mode theory.<ref name=NAS>{{cite journal|author=Shapiro, Stephen|author2=Axe, John|author3=Shirane, Haruo|author4=Shirane, Tatsuo|title=Gen Shirane (1924–2005)|journal=Biographical Memoirs|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|year=2017|pages=1–12| url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/shirane-gen.pdf}} (p. 5)</ref>

Shirane was a leading international authority on neutron spectroscopy in solid-state physics, including magnetic materials and [[high-temperature superconductivity|high-T<sub>c</sub> superconductivity]]. He trained many younger physicists in neutron scattering and effectively promoted collaborations between Japan and the USA. He was the author or co-author of over 750 scientific publications with nearly 40,000 citations by the year of his death. His [[h-index]] was 103.<ref name=IEEE>{{cite web|website=IEEE, Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics, and Frequency Control|url=http://www.ieee-uffc.org/memoria/gen-shirane|title=In memoriam. Gen Shirane|date=2016-10-10}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* 1973 — Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize, American Physical Society
* 1973 — Warren Award of the [[American Crystallographic Association]]<ref>{{cite web|title=ACA Award Descriptions|website=American Crystallographic Association|url=https://www.amercrystalassn.org/awards/|access-date=2019-09-22|archive-date=2019-04-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404195943/https://www.amercrystalassn.org/awards|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 1989 — Member of the National Academy of Sciences
* 1989 — [[United States Department of Energy|DOE]] Award for Outstanding Scientific Accomplishment in Solid State Physics
* 1991 — Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences
* 2003 — Award for Outstanding Accomplishment, Japanese Society for Neutron Science<ref name=IEEE/>
